name: chocolate ganache
instructions:
A cocoa-butter-forward chocolate ganache that lets you dial the darkness with bakers chocolate rather than trying (and failing) to dilute bakers chocolate with cream alone.

=== BASE APPROACH — MILK CHOCOLATE + BAKERS FOR DARKENING ===

1. Melt 1-2 tbsp of SALTED BUTTER in a skillet on LOW heat (for flavor, not structure).
2. Add MILK CHOCOLATE CHIPS. Stir vigorously as they melt into the butter.
3. Add BAKERS CHOCOLATE (60%) in VERY CONSERVATIVE amounts to darken as desired. See notes on why this direction (milk → darker) works and the reverse (bakers → lighter) doesn't.
4. Pour in enough HEAVY CREAM so the chocolate doesn't burn — but no more. Less cream = thicker ganache (preferred); more cream = runnier. Not many rules here; adjust to taste.
5. Keep stirring on low until smooth and glossy.

=== ALTERNATIVE APPROACH — WHITE CHOCOLATE BASE + BAKERS FOR SPECTRUM ===

Same procedure, but start with WHITE CHOCOLATE CHIPS as the base instead of milk chocolate chips. Then mix in bakers chocolate for darkening. Gives you EVEN MORE SPECTRUM CONTROL — you can dial the ganache anywhere from pale-white through medium-tan to dark. Reach for this when you want a lighter finished ganache, or when you want a two-tone visual against a dark cake.
notes:
=== WHY MILK/WHITE CHOCOLATE + BAKERS INSTEAD OF BAKERS + CREAM ===

Bakers chocolate (60%) is TOO DARK on its own for a finished ganache. It's tempting to reach for cream to dilute the flavor, but cream ALONE can't do it — you need more COCOA BUTTER, which milk chocolate and white chocolate have in higher ratios than bakers does. So the correct move is to build from milk (or white) chocolate as the cocoa-butter-rich base and add bakers conservatively to darken, rather than starting with bakers and trying to lighten it.

This is the whole framing of the recipe: control darkness with COCOA BUTTER RATIOS, not with cream volume.

=== CREAM AMOUNT — NOT MANY RULES ===

Enough cream so the chocolate doesn't burn — that's the floor. Above that, more cream = runnier ganache; less cream = thicker. I don't like runny ganache so I lean sparse. There aren't many rules here; adjust to taste and to what you're topping.

=== DOUBLE BOILER IS TRADITIONAL — I JUST STIR A SKILLET ON LOW VIGOROUSLY ===

The canonical technique for chocolate melting is a double boiler (glass bowl over simmering water) to prevent scorching. I skip that and use a regular skillet on LOW heat with vigorous stirring. Works fine as long as the heat stays low and you don't stop stirring. The cream helps here too — once it's in, the chocolate has enough moisture to buffer against scorching.

=== DUTCH PROCESSED COCOA WORKS BEST; ESPRESSO POWDER IS THE FALLBACK ===

BEST ADDITION — DUTCH PROCESSED COCOA POWDER: works best in this ganache. Deepens the chocolate register without adding sweetness or fat, and its smoother/less-acidic character fits the cocoa-butter-forward base.

FALLBACK — A LITTLE ESPRESSO POWDER: if you don't have dutch process cocoa, a small amount of espresso powder helps make the ganache read more dessert-like. Not the same effect as dutch cocoa (espresso adds a coffee note rather than deepening the chocolate), but it lifts the ganache out of a plain-melted-chocolate register.

=== SALTED BUTTER, JUST A LITTLE ===

1-2 tbsp salted butter for FLAVOR, not structure. Salted specifically — plays against the chocolate's sweetness. Structural work is done by the chocolate + cream; butter is a flavor-only addition here.

=== DARKER CHOCOLATE CLASHES WITH LEMON; WHITE OR LIGHT MILK CHOCOLATE WORKS ===

A general principle worth noting for pairings: darker chocolate doesn't go well with lemon, which is a common pastry flavor profile (lemon curd, lemon pound cake, lemon tarts, etc.). WHITE CHOCOLATE or LIGHT MILK CHOCOLATE does pair with lemon.

Applied here: if you're making ganache for a lemon-forward dessert (see french-yogurt-cake, greek-yogurt-lemon-pound-cake), reach for the WHITE CHOCOLATE base version of this recipe and go easy on the bakers chocolate darkening. A dark-forward ganache would fight the lemon; a white or pale-tan ganache extends the lemon-and-dairy register cleanly.

=== SERVING — CAKE TOPPING, ESPECIALLY CHEESECAKE ===

Ganache goes well on top of any cake, but ESPECIALLY CHEESECAKE. The cream-cheese-forward base of a cheesecake pairs cleanly with the cocoa-butter-forward ganache — same dairy register, the ganache adds chocolate depth without competing with the cake's texture.

Cross-references: new-york-cheesecake (the natural pairing), chocolate-cake (works but the cake already has chocolate — see caramel-frosting for that pairing instead).

=== SIBLING RECIPES ===

- caramel-frosting: another dessert topping, dairy + sugar caramelization instead of chocolate + cream. Different register; both belong in the topping/frosting family.
- buttercream-frosting: sturdier / more structural topping. Ganache is looser and more free-form; buttercream holds shape.
- cream-cheese-frosting: closer in register to ganache (both dairy-forward). Ganache adds chocolate; cream cheese adds tang.
